 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Soccer", "Rugby", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) searching six databases on 1 May 2025, with 582 titles and abstracts screened, 74 full texts assessed and seven studies included. Across these studies, uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers to return to sport and physical activity, while confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The evidence base is seven studies drawn from soccer, rugby union, Gaelic and Australian football, at mixed levels of play, and the synthesis is narrative with no effect estimates. It cannot show that psychosocial factors cause differences in return to sport.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat these barriers and facilitators as measured predictors of return to sport, when they are perceived experiences reported by a few studies and the review does not show that changing them improves outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Meredith S, Farley JB, Hunt J, Dent E. The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:148.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01118-6",
  "abstract": "Scoping review of seven studies on psychosocial factors and return to physical activity and sport in female football players after anterior cruciate ligament injury. Fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were barriers, while confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were facilitators.",
  "tldr": "For female footballers after an ACL injury, fear, uncertainty, low confidence and weak social support were reported as barriers to return. Confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were reported as helpers, so build these into the return plan alongside the physical milestones.",
  "methods": "Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR with a prospective protocol. Six databases (SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo and Embase) were searched on 1 May 2025, and two reviewers screened records against eligibility criteria: original research on psychosocial factors and return to sport or physical activity in female players of any football code with an ACL injury, managed surgically or non-surgically, and mean participant age of 18 or older. Findings were synthesized narratively into themes.",
  "findings": "Seven studies were included. Across them, uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers to return at a lower competition level and to physical activity. Confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators, helping players return at their preinjury level or at a lower level.",
  "limitations": "Only seven studies were included, and the findings are narrative themes from perceived experiences rather than effect estimates. The authors call for more high-quality research focused specifically on female footballers, with greater consideration of sex and gender in study design.",
  "practicalImplications": "Return-to-sport planning for female footballers after ACL injury should include fear, confidence and social support alongside physical milestones. The authors discuss psychologically informed, exposure-based approaches to fear of reinjury, but the review does not test any screening tool or intervention.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff working with female footballers should track confidence, fear and social support alongside physical testing, because these were reported to shape how players return to their level. The evidence is perceptual and does not set performance targets.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to return-to-sport planning in female footballers after ACL injury: fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were reported as barriers, and confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity as facilitators. It cannot set return criteria, and it does not show whether addressing these factors changes return rates."
 }
}
{
 "id": "Q12",
 "sourceFile": "Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) of resistance training after primary ACL reconstruction in adults or adolescents, comparing blood flow restriction, isokinetic, eccentric and other modalities with standard multimodal rehabilitation. Blood flow restriction ranked first for quadriceps strength (SMD 0.40 vs standard rehabilitation, 95% CI 0.07-0.73) and quadriceps mass (SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53), and eccentric training ranked first for quality of life (SMD 1.31 vs standard rehabilitation, 95% CI 0.01-2.63); isokinetic training ranked highest for knee function, but differences among active modalities were not significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Several contrasts rest on few trials (PT and IKT in particular), protocols, cuff pressures, loading and follow-up varied widely, and the comparator was usual rehabilitation rather than a single standard. The sample was not restricted to athletes, so the trial populations are not described as athletes in the source.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the isokinetic SUCRA ranking for knee function as proof that isokinetic training is the best option, when the authors state that pairwise differences among active modalities were not significant and there is no clear evidence of superiority.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Chen J, Wu Y, Xu H, Ren Y, Yang R, Yao S, et al. Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Physiol. 2026;17:1792091.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fphys.2026.1792091",
  "abstract": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) comparing resistance training modalities after primary ACL reconstruction on quadriceps strength, quadriceps mass, knee function and health-related quality of life, using SUCRA rankings.",
  "tldr": "Blood flow restriction training ranked best for quadriceps strength and mass compared with usual rehabilitation, and eccentric training for quality of life. Isokinetic training ranked highest for knee function, but no active modality clearly beat the others on that outcome, so choose the modality to match the target.",
  "methods": "Searches of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science and Google Scholar to 30 September 2025 for randomized trials in adults or adolescents after primary ACL reconstruction that compared resistance-based modalities with standard multimodal rehabilitation or with each other. Outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences, modalities were ranked by SUCRA, and network consistency was assessed with a design-by-treatment interaction model.",
  "findings": "Twenty-two trials (n = 797) were included. Blood flow restriction training ranked first for quadriceps strength (SUCRA 81.7; SMD 0.40, 95% CI 0.07-0.73 vs standard rehabilitation) and quadriceps mass (SUCRA 79.1; SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53 vs standard rehabilitation). Isokinetic training had the highest ranking for knee function (SUCRA 87.7), but pairwise differences among active modalities were not statistically significant. Eccentric training ranked first for quality of life (SUCRA 87.4; SMD 1.31, 95% CI 0.01-2.63 vs standard rehabilitation).",
  "limitations": "The network was uneven, with few trials for some contrasts (PT and IKT in particular), which limits precision for head-to-head comparisons. Heterogeneity in intervention parameters, outcome instruments and follow-up windows could not be modeled with study-level data, and residual confounding is possible. Time since surgery, graft type and kinetic chain configuration were inconsistently reported.",
  "practicalImplications": "Match the resistance modality to the outcome: blood flow restriction training for quadriceps strength and mass, and eccentric training for quality of life, both compared with usual rehabilitation. Do not treat isokinetic training as clearly superior for knee function, since the pairwise differences among active modalities were not significant.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance and rehabilitation staff can use the ranking to choose a resistance emphasis that fits a quadriceps or quality-of-life goal after ACL reconstruction. The review does not test sport-specific performance outcomes such as sprinting, jumping or change of direction.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to rehabilitation after primary ACL reconstruction, where blood flow restriction ranked first for quadriceps strength and mass. The review does not measure time to return to sport, sport readiness or re-injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return."
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for concussion - a systematic review and meta-analysis for the Female, woman and girl_or Athlete Injury pRevention (FAIR) consensus.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis for the Female, woman and girl and/or Athlete Injury pRevention (FAIR) consensus' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby", "Ice Hockey", "American Football", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Female Athletes", "Youth / Adolescent", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review with meta-analyses and GRADE ratings of 108 studies (67 on prevention strategies, 41 on modifiable risk factors), of which 40 (37%) reported female, woman or girl-specific estimates. Headgear was associated with a lower concussion rate (IRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.99), eyewear was not protective (IRR 1.08, 95% CI 0.69-1.68), and artificial turf vs grass showed no difference (IRR 0.95, 95% CI 0.62-1.45); all three were very low certainty.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most studies were not female-specific, and the headgear estimate comes from very low certainty cohort evidence in adolescent lacrosse and soccer. The review cannot support confident recommendations for female, woman or girl athletes overall.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat headgear as an established concussion prevention measure for female athletes, when the only protective estimate is very low certainty and comes from adolescent lacrosse and soccer.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Shill IJ, Shepherd HA, Eliason PH, Kolstad AT, Heyward O, Martens G, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis for the Female, woman and girl and/or Athlete Injury pRevention (FAIR) consensus. Br J Sports Med. 2025, pp. 1599-1616.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2025-109915",
  "abstract": "Systematic review with meta-analyses and GRADE of 108 studies on prevention strategies (67) and modifiable risk factors (41) for sport-related concussion and head impact events in female, woman and girl athletes. Evidence was mostly limited or very low certainty, and only 37% of studies gave female-specific estimates.",
  "tldr": "Evidence for concussion prevention strategies and risk factors in female, woman and girl athletes is mostly limited. The only protective signal is very low certainty support for headgear in adolescent lacrosse and soccer, while eyewear and artificial turf showed no protective effect.",
  "methods": "Systematic review with meta-analyses following PRISMA, with GRADE certainty ratings. Medline, CINAHL, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, ERIC, CENTRAL and CDSR were searched for primary studies comparing prevention strategies or modifiable risk factors with sport-related concussion or head impact and acceleration event outcomes. Female, woman or girl-specific estimates were extracted where reported, and three meta-analyses were run (headgear, eyewear, artificial turf vs grass).",
  "findings": "108 studies were included (67 prevention, 41 modifiable risk factors); 40 (37%) reported female, woman or girl-specific estimates. Headgear was associated with a lower concussion rate (IRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50-0.99; very low certainty). Eyewear was not protective (IRR 1.08, 95% CI 0.69-1.68; very low certainty), and artificial turf vs grass showed no difference (IRR 0.95, 95% CI 0.62-1.45; very low certainty). The consensus found limited evidence for most strategies and risk factors.",
  "limitations": "Only 37% of studies gave female, woman or girl-specific estimates, and most pooled data combined sexes, so sex-specific conclusions are weak. None of the studies reporting female-specific estimates examined unintended consequences. Heterogeneity in outcomes and interventions meant that most results were reported without pooling, and only three meta-analyses were possible.",
  "practicalImplications": "Headgear may be considered for adolescent female lacrosse and soccer players only as a low-certainty option. Eyewear and artificial turf should not be relied on to reduce concussion, and most other strategies and risk factors need better female-specific data before recommendations are made.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance and medical staff should not change equipment or playing surfaces for concussion reduction on the strength of this review, beyond the very low certainty headgear finding in adolescent lacrosse and soccer.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to concussion prevention rather than return to play. The review does not study recovery or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform when an athlete can return after a concussion."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q15",
 "sourceFile": "Acute-chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports - a multilevel meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and three-level multilevel meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies and trials in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, and elevated acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) showed a small-to-moderate association with injury risk (Hedges g 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54; I2 = 95.8%), stronger for contact and non-contact injuries and not significant for time-loss injuries.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Heterogeneity was very high (I2 = 95.8%), several moderator analyses rested on few studies, and ACWR calculation methods, time windows, load metrics and injury definitions varied. The review shows association only and cannot establish causation or prediction.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled g of 0.35 as a 35% increase in injury risk, which the authors explicitly reject, and treat ACWR as a stand-alone injury predictor, which they also reject.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Ding L, Weldon A, Xu J, Malone S, Sampaio J, Zhang Z, et al. Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1896651.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896651",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the association between acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, showing a small-to-moderate association with injury (g = 0.35).",
  "tldr": "In team-sport athletes, a high acute:chronic workload ratio was associated with a small-to-moderate increase in injury risk, most clearly for contact and non-contact injuries. The authors conclude it is a contextual monitoring indicator to use within a multi-marker load-management approach, not a stand-alone predictor.",
  "methods": "Four electronic databases searched from inception to October 2024. Prospective cohort studies or trials in team-sport athletes reporting ACWR and injury outcomes were included; effect sizes were converted to Hedges g and pooled with a three-level random-effects model, with moderator analyses by injury type and other study characteristics. Registered in PROSPERO (CRD420245127618).",
  "findings": "Of 41 eligible studies, 16 studies involving 797 athletes were included in the meta-analysis. Elevated ACWR was associated with higher injury risk (g = 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54; I2 = 95.8%). Associations were stronger for contact and non-contact injuries, and not significant for time-loss injuries or other moderators.",
  "limitations": "Residual statistical dependence may remain when several outcomes, time windows or workload metrics come from the same cohort. Several moderator analyses rested on few studies, reducing power to detect subgroup differences. Load metrics, time windows and injury definitions varied across the included studies, and heterogeneity was very high.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use ACWR as a contextual monitoring indicator within an individualized, multi-marker load-management system, not as a stand-alone causal or predictive model. The authors state that the pooled effect should not be read as a 35% increase in injury risk.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can track ACWR alongside other load and wellness markers to watch workload trends, but should not use it as a stand-alone injury predictor. The review addresses injury risk, not performance outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Limited relevance to return to sport: the review covers injury risk in team-sport athletes, not rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loading or clearance."
 }
}
{
 "id": "Q16",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies comparing acute caffeine with placebo on repeated sprint ability (RSA), pooled as weighted mean differences. Caffeine increased RSA peak power output (WMD 5.28, 95% CI 2.49-8.07), with a larger effect at doses of 6 mg/kg or more (WMD 6.67, 95% CI 3.32-10.02) than lower doses (WMD 2.16, 95% CI -2.87 to 7.19, not significant) and a larger effect in cycling (WMD 8.77) than running (WMD 4.56) protocols.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review rests on 13 studies with varied caffeine forms, doses and RSA protocols, and habitual caffeine intake and training status were not fully controlled. It measures peak power in RSA tests, not sport-specific match or competition performance.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could apply the pooled caffeine benefit to any dose and any sprint sport, when the gain comes mostly from doses of 6 mg/kg or more and cycling-based tests, and the lower-dose estimate crosses zero.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Wang Y, Su W, Zhang S, Zhao L, Lv Y, Gu B, et al. Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nutrients. 2025;17:3475.",
  "doi": "10.3390/nu17213475",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on acute caffeine and repeated sprint ability. Caffeine improved peak power output compared with placebo, with larger effects at doses of 6 mg/kg or more and in cycling-based protocols, and no significant sex difference in the pooled analysis.",
  "tldr": "Caffeine taken about 60 minutes before exercise improved repeated sprint peak power, and the benefit was clearest at 6 mg/kg or more. The pooled effect was similar in males and females, with no significant sex difference.",
  "methods": "PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis of PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane Library, Web of Science and Scopus, comparing acute caffeine with placebo on RSA. Data were pooled as weighted mean differences with 95% CI, with subgroup analyses by sex, dose and exercise modality. Protocol prospectively registered in PROSPERO.",
  "findings": "Thirteen studies were included. Caffeine significantly increased RSA peak power output versus placebo (WMD 5.28, 95% CI 2.49-8.07; p = 0.0002). The effect was significant in males (WMD 13.11, 95% CI 5.63-20.59) and females (WMD 4.03, 95% CI 1.10-6.97), with no significant sex difference in the pooled analysis. Doses of 6 mg/kg or more (WMD 6.67) outperformed lower doses (WMD 2.16, p = 0.40), and cycling protocols (WMD 8.77) outperformed running protocols (WMD 4.56).",
  "limitations": "Caffeine was given in several forms (powder, capsules, mouth rinse, caffeinated drinks), and the limited number of eligible studies restricted dose stratification. The authors call for research on training status, habitual caffeine intake and sport-specific RSA protocols, since current protocols may not match running-based sports well.",
  "practicalImplications": "Caffeine at 6 mg/kg or more, taken about 60 minutes before repeated sprint work, is the dose the authors identify as an evidence-based strategy to improve repeated sprint peak power. Lower doses did not show a clear benefit in this pooled analysis.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance and sports nutrition staff can use caffeine at 6 mg/kg or more, about 60 minutes before exercise, as an evidence-based option for repeated sprint peak power. The outcome is RSA peak power in test protocols, so sport-specific effects still need checking.",
  "rtp": "Not designed for return to sport: the included studies tested RSA performance in healthy adults, so the review cannot inform caffeine use during rehabilitation or after injury."
 }
}

4	Are There Sex Disparities in Return
5	to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament
6	Reconstruction?
7	A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
8	Darby Amelia Elliott,*y  Saran Singh Gill,z BSc ,
9	and Chinmay Madhukar Gupte,§ PhD, MA, BMBCh (Oxon)
10	Investigation performed at Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom
11	
12	Background: Sex disparities in return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remain
13	poorly reported. Female athletes may demonstrate higher rates of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries than male athletes
14	yet exhibit lower RTS rates.
15	Purpose: To compare postoperative RTS outcomes between male and female patients after primary ACLR.
16	Study Design: Systematic review; Level of evidence, 4.
17	Methods: A systematic search of the PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science databases was conducted from
18	database inception through September 2025, following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-
19	Analyses) guidelines. Studies directly comparing RTS outcomes between males and females after primary ACLR with 12 months
20	of follow-up were included. Data were synthesized using an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis. Odds ratios with 95%
21	confidence intervals were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences for continuous variables.
22	Results: In total, 25 studies including 7183 athletes (2892 females, 4291 males) met the inclusion criteria. Female athletes dem-
23	onstrated significantly lower odds of RTS at 12 months (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.62-0.92; P = .005) and up to and including 24 months
24	(OR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.61-0.85; P \ .001). No significant sex-based differences were observed for RTS to competition or return to
25	preinjury levels.
26	Conclusion: Female athletes are significantly less likely to RTS after ACLR during the critical midterm recovery period. These
27	findings highlight the need for sex-specific rehabilitation and psychological support strategies to optimize RTS outcomes in
28	female athletes.
29	Keywords: ACL; anterior cruciate ligament; ACLR; return to sport; female; sex

Clinical Sports Medicine Update


Are There Sex Disparities in Return
to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Reconstruction?
A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
Darby Amelia Elliott,*y  Saran Singh Gill,z BSc ,
and Chinmay Madhukar Gupte,§ PhD, MA, BMBCh (Oxon)
Investigation performed at Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom

Background: Sex disparities in return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remain
poorly reported. Female athletes may demonstrate higher rates of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries than male athletes
yet exhibit lower RTS rates.
Purpose: To compare postoperative RTS outcomes between male and female patients after primary ACLR.
Study Design: Systematic review; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A systematic search of the PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science databases was conducted from
database inception through September 2025, following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-
Analyses) guidelines. Studies directly comparing RTS outcomes between males and females after primary ACLR with 12 months
of follow-up were included. Data were synthesized using an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis. Odds ratios with 95%
confidence intervals were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences for continuous variables.
Results: In total, 25 studies including 7183 athletes (2892 females, 4291 males) met the inclusion criteria. Female athletes dem-
onstrated significantly lower odds of RTS at 12 months (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.62-0.92; P = .005) and up to and including 24 months
(OR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.61-0.85; P \ .001). No significant sex-based differences were observed for RTS to competition or return to
preinjury levels.
Conclusion: Female athletes are significantly less likely to RTS after ACLR during the critical midterm recovery period. These
findings highlight the need for sex-specific rehabilitation and psychological support strategies to optimize RTS outcomes in
female athletes.
Keywords: ACL; anterior cruciate ligament; ACLR; return to sport; female; sex

19	  Abstract
20	  Background The existing body of evidence referring to the return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes and psychological
21	  readiness to return to sport after revision compared to the primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction has
22	  not yet been comprehensively synthesized.
23	  Objective To examine RTS outcomes and psychological readiness to return to sport after revision compared to the
24	  primary ACL reconstruction.
25	  Methods A comprehensive search of Web of Science, EMBASE, and PubMed was carried out up to November 15,
26	  2024. Observational studies that compared revision and primary ACL reconstruction regarding RTS outcomes and
27	  psychological readiness to return to sport were considered adequate for inclusion. The Methodological Index for
28	  Non-Randomized Studies and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation were used to
29	  assess methodological quality as well as the overall strength and quality of evidence of involved studies, respectively.
30	  Results A total of 19 studies fulfilled the eligibility criteria and were included in the quantitative analysis. There were
31	  3209 athletes with a history of revision and primary ACL reconstruction (mean age: 26.0 ± 6.5 years; 78% males). The
32	  main findings indicated that individuals who were subjected to revision ACL reconstruction had slightly lower odds of
33	  RTS (-6%; odds ratio (OR) = 0.66 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.49 to 0.89]), slightly lower odds of RTS at the preinjury
34	  level of competition (-5%; OR = 0.52 [95% CI 0.36 to 0.76]), slightly prolonged RTS time (1.2 months; standardized
35	  mean differences (SMD) = 0.38 [95% CI 0.12 to -0.63]), and moderately lower psychological readiness to return to sport
36	  (-14.2 points; SMD = -0.75 [95% CI -1.14 to -0.36]) relative to their counterparts who were subjected to the primary
37	  ACL surgery.

61	 Conclusions Athletes who underwent the revision ACL surgery had a 6% reduced rate of RTS, 5% lower rates of
62	 RTS at the preinjury level of competition, 1.2 months extended RTS time, and 14.2 points decreased psychological
63	 readiness to return to sport relative to the respondents with a history of the primary ACL reconstruction.
64	 PROSPERO registration number CRD42024600347.
65	 Key Points
66	   • Athletes who underwent the revision anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) surgery had 6% and 5% reduced
67	      rates to return-to-sport (RTS), and to RTS at the preinjury level of competition, respectively, with 1.2 months
68	      extended RTS time compared to their counterparts with a history of primary ACL reconstruction.
69	   • The obtained results demonstrated that psychological readiness to return to sport was 14.2 points lower after
70	      revision relative to the primary ACL surgery.
71	   • The novel recovery approach is recommended for athletes with revision ACL reconstruction, consisting of
72	      exercise sessions and psychological interventions to improve examined parameters and prevent additional
73	      knee injuries.
74	 Keywords Exercise psychology, Knee injury, Return to play, Return to play time, Surgery

Return-to-Sport Outcomes and Psychological
Readiness to Return to Sport After Revision
Compared to the Primary Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic
Review and Meta-Analysis
Marko Manojlovic1* , Vukadin Milankov2 , Roberto Roklicer1,3 , Tatjana Trivic1 , Aleksander Veraksa4 ,
Antonino Bianco5 and Patrik Drid1


  Abstract
  Background The existing body of evidence referring to the return-to-sport (RTS) outcomes and psychological
  readiness to return to sport after revision compared to the primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction has
  not yet been comprehensively synthesized.
  Objective To examine RTS outcomes and psychological readiness to return to sport after revision compared to the
  primary ACL reconstruction.
  Methods A comprehensive search of Web of Science, EMBASE, and PubMed was carried out up to November 15,
  2024. Observational studies that compared revision and primary ACL reconstruction regarding RTS outcomes and
  psychological readiness to return to sport were considered adequate for inclusion. The Methodological Index for
  Non-Randomized Studies and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation were used to
  assess methodological quality as well as the overall strength and quality of evidence of involved studies, respectively.
  Results A total of 19 studies fulfilled the eligibility criteria and were included in the quantitative analysis. There were
  3209 athletes with a history of revision and primary ACL reconstruction (mean age: 26.0 ± 6.5 years; 78% males). The
  main findings indicated that individuals who were subjected to revision ACL reconstruction had slightly lower odds of
  RTS (-6%; odds ratio (OR) = 0.66 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.49 to 0.89]), slightly lower odds of RTS at the preinjury
  level of competition (-5%; OR = 0.52 [95% CI 0.36 to 0.76]), slightly prolonged RTS time (1.2 months; standardized
  mean differences (SMD) = 0.38 [95% CI 0.12 to -0.63]), and moderately lower psychological readiness to return to sport
  (-14.2 points; SMD = -0.75 [95% CI -1.14 to -0.36]) relative to their counterparts who were subjected to the primary
  ACL surgery.

 Conclusions Athletes who underwent the revision ACL surgery had a 6% reduced rate of RTS, 5% lower rates of
 RTS at the preinjury level of competition, 1.2 months extended RTS time, and 14.2 points decreased psychological
 readiness to return to sport relative to the respondents with a history of the primary ACL reconstruction.
 PROSPERO registration number CRD42024600347.
 Key Points
   • Athletes who underwent the revision anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) surgery had 6% and 5% reduced
      rates to return-to-sport (RTS), and to RTS at the preinjury level of competition, respectively, with 1.2 months
      extended RTS time compared to their counterparts with a history of primary ACL reconstruction.
   • The obtained results demonstrated that psychological readiness to return to sport was 14.2 points lower after
      revision relative to the primary ACL surgery.
   • The novel recovery approach is recommended for athletes with revision ACL reconstruction, consisting of
      exercise sessions and psychological interventions to improve examined parameters and prevent additional
      knee injuries.

9	The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning
10	to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female
11	Football Players After Anterior Cruciate
12	Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review
13	Skye Meredith1* , Jessica B. Farley1 , Jane Hunt2   and Elsa Dent3   
14	
15	
16	
17	  Abstract
18	  Background Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are an increasingly common knee injury in sport requiring
19	  quick direction changes, such as the football codes. Return to physical activity and sport following an ACL injury pre-
20	  dominantly focuses on achieving objective milestones to resolve physical impairments, with sex differences reported.
21	  However, irrespective of management approach following an ACL injury, many athletes do not return to the same
22	  level of sport, if at all, warranting the need to consider psychological and social factors.
23	  Aim The aim of this scoping review was to investigate the role of psychosocial factors in females participating in any
24	  football code after an ACL injury, and the impact on return to physical activity and sport.
25	  Methods A systematic search of six electronic databases (SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo,
26	  and Embase) was conducted on 1 May 2025. Two reviewers independently screened articles against the eligibility
27	  criteria to include original research articles that explored the impact of psychosocial factors on return to sport (RTS)
28	  or physical activity in females playing any football code with an ACL injury managed surgically or non-surgically.
29	  Studies were eligible where participants had a mean age of 18 years or older. Data extraction and narrative synthesis
30	  of included studies was undertaken and themes identified to address the research aim.
31	  Results Full-text articles (n = 74) were assessed for eligibility following screening of titles and abstracts (n = 582);
32	  seven eligible studies were included. Across the studies, psychosocial barriers and facilitators were perceived to influ-
33	  ence RTS at either preinjury or lower competition levels, as well as physical activity, in female footballers. Uncertainty,
34	  fear, lack of confidence, and poor social support were identified as perceived barriers to RTS contributing to return
35	  at a lower level of competition and the alteration, limitation, or avoidance of physical activity among female football-
36	  ers. Whilst confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were identified as perceived facilitators
37	  of RTS, helping to build readiness and supporting female footballers to return at their preinjury level or a lower level
38	  of competition.
39	  Conclusion Psychosocial factors appear to play an important role in RTS and physical activity following ACL injury
40	  in female football players, acting as both barriers and facilitators to recovery. Further high-quality research focussed
41	  specifically on female footballers is needed to better understand these relationships and inform targeted screening
42	  and interventions.
43

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW                                                                                                                                           Open Access

The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning
to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female
Football Players After Anterior Cruciate
Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review
Skye Meredith1* , Jessica B. Farley1 , Jane Hunt2   and Elsa Dent3   



  Abstract
  Background Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are an increasingly common knee injury in sport requiring
  quick direction changes, such as the football codes. Return to physical activity and sport following an ACL injury pre-
  dominantly focuses on achieving objective milestones to resolve physical impairments, with sex differences reported.
  However, irrespective of management approach following an ACL injury, many athletes do not return to the same
  level of sport, if at all, warranting the need to consider psychological and social factors.
  Aim The aim of this scoping review was to investigate the role of psychosocial factors in females participating in any
  football code after an ACL injury, and the impact on return to physical activity and sport.
  Methods A systematic search of six electronic databases (SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo,
  and Embase) was conducted on 1 May 2025. Two reviewers independently screened articles against the eligibility
  criteria to include original research articles that explored the impact of psychosocial factors on return to sport (RTS)
  or physical activity in females playing any football code with an ACL injury managed surgically or non-surgically.
  Studies were eligible where participants had a mean age of 18 years or older. Data extraction and narrative synthesis
  of included studies was undertaken and themes identified to address the research aim.
  Results Full-text articles (n = 74) were assessed for eligibility following screening of titles and abstracts (n = 582);
  seven eligible studies were included. Across the studies, psychosocial barriers and facilitators were perceived to influ-
  ence RTS at either preinjury or lower competition levels, as well as physical activity, in female footballers. Uncertainty,
  fear, lack of confidence, and poor social support were identified as perceived barriers to RTS contributing to return
  at a lower level of competition and the alteration, limitation, or avoidance of physical activity among female football-
  ers. Whilst confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were identified as perceived facilitators
  of RTS, helping to build readiness and supporting female footballers to return at their preinjury level or a lower level
  of competition.
  Conclusion Psychosocial factors appear to play an important role in RTS and physical activity following ACL injury
  in female football players, acting as both barriers and facilitators to recovery. Further high-quality research focussed
  specifically on female footballers is needed to better understand these relationships and inform targeted screening
  and interventions.

  Key Points

    • Psychosocial factors have a perceived impact on female football players returning to sport and/or physical activ-
      ity after ACL injury, acting as barriers and facilitators.
    • Uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence, and poor social support were identified as perceived barriers to return
      to sport, contributing to return at a lower level of competition and the alteration, limitation, or avoidance of phys-
      ical activity among female footballers.
    • Confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were identified as perceived facilitators
      of return to sport, supporting female footballers to return at their preinjury level or a lower level of competition.
    • Incorporating psychosocial screening into rehabilitation may help support return to sport outcomes in female
      footballers following ACL injury.

60	                                                Caffeine, the primary bioactive compound found in widely consumed beverages such
61	(https://creativecommons.org/              as coffee, tea, and cocoa, acts as a central nervous system stimulant and adenosine receptor
62	licenses/by/4.0/).                         antagonist [1]. It is rapidly absorbed and exerts diverse physiological effects, including
63	
64	
65	Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                          https://doi.org/10.3390/nu17213475
66	 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                              2 of 17
67	
68	
69	
70	                           reducing fatigue, enhancing lipolysis, and increasing alertness [2–4]. Although generally
71	                           considered safe at typical consumption levels, excessive intake may cause adverse effects
72	                           such as anxiety, insomnia, and gastrointestinal discomfort [5–7]. Owing to its pronounced
73	                           physiological actions, caffeine has long been a subject of extensive research in the context
74	                           of performance enhancement and remains one of the most widely used legal psychoactive
75	                           substances worldwide.
76	                                 In the field of sports science, caffeine is recognized as a potent ergogenic aid capable
77	                           of augmenting athletic performance through multiple mechanisms. Early studies demon-
78	                           strated that caffeine enhances aerobic endurance primarily by promoting fat oxidation
79	                           and conserving muscle glycogen stores [8,9]. Subsequent research extended these observa-
80	                           tions, indicating that caffeine may also improve anaerobic endurance and high-intensity
81	                           exercise performance through multiple mechanisms, including reduced pain perception,
82	                           enhanced muscle contractility, and improved neural drive [10,11]. Notably, caffeine was
83	                           only removed from the World Anti-Doping Agency’s list of prohibited substances in 2004,
84	                           thereby legitimizing its use as an ergogenic aid among elite athletes. Since then, caffeine-
85	                           containing energy drinks have emerged as a popular vehicle for delivering this ergogenic
86	                           aid. These beverages typically combine substantial amounts of caffeine with additional
87	                           ingredients such as carbohydrates, B vitamins, and taurine, thereby providing an auxil-
88	                           iary energy source during exercise [12,13]. However, the primary ergogenic benefits are
89	                           largely attributed to their high caffeine content, with nearly half of professional athletes
90	                           reportedly using caffeine-based supplements to enhance performance [14]. According to
91	                           the International Society of Sports Nutrition, caffeine consumption approximately 60 min
92	                           prior to exercise can effectively improve various aspects of athletic performance, including
93	                           endurance capacity, high-intensity effort, and muscular strength [15].
94	                                 Repeated sprint ability (RSA) is a performance parameter that depends primarily on
95	                           the adenosine triphosphate-creatine phosphate (ATP-CP) energy system and plays a crucial
96	                           role in high-intensity intermittent sports such as basketball, soccer, and rugby [16–19].
97	                           However, the ergogenic potential of acute caffeine ingestion for improving RSA remains
98	                           controversial. Several studies have reported that acute caffeine supplementation enhances
99	                           RSA by increasing both peak power output (PPO) and mean power output (MPO) [20,21].
100	                           In contrast, other studies have failed to detect such benefits. For instance, Bernardo et al. [22]
101	                           observed no significant differences in PPO or MPO between caffeine and placebo conditions
102	                           in male participants. Similarly, Houda et al. [23] reported that an acute caffeine dose of
103	                           3 mg/kg body weight (BW) did not significantly influence RSA in young female athletes,
104	                           whereas higher doses of 6 or 9 mg/kg BW improved performance by reducing both the
105	                           fastest and mean sprint time, suggesting a potential dose–response effect. Conversely,
106	                           another research demonstrated that even a 3 mg/kg BW caffeine dose was sufficient to
107	                           enhance both PPO and MPO during repeated sprints [24]. Collectively, these inconsistent
108	                           findings indicate that the ergogenic effects of caffeine on RSA remain equivocal and may
109	                           be influenced by interindividual differences in caffeine sensitivity [25].
110	                                 Existing meta-analyses examining the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA have
111	                           also produced divergent conclusions. For instance, Gomez-Bruton et al. [26] reported no
112	                           significant effect of caffeine on RSA in females athletes, whereas López-Torres et al. [27]
113	                           demonstrated a positive ergogenic effect. Similarly, Lopes-Silva et al. [28] found that acute
114	                           caffeine ingestion did not significantly improve RSA, while another meta-analysis revealed
115	                           that caffeine markedly enhanced high-intensity performance in elite athletes during both
116	                           real or simulated competitions [29]. These discrepancies among meta-analytic findings may
117	                           stem from methodological limitations, such as the inclusion of only female participants, the
118	                           absence of dosage stratification, and inadequate control for habitual caffeine consumption.

123	                                Therefore, to address these inconsistencies and methodological gaps, the present
124	                           systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate the effects of
125	                           acute caffeine ingestion on RSA.

127	                           2. Materials and Methods
128	                           2.1. Design
129	                                This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the
130	                           Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluation and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guide-
131	                           lines [30]. The study protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective
132	                           Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD420251150247).
133	
134	                           2.2. Search Strategy
135	                                A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane
136	                           Library, Web of science, and Scopus databases from their inception to 6 September 2025.
137	                           The search strategy employed the keywords and MESH terms “caffeine” and “repeated
138	                           sprint ability” (Table S1). Additionally, reference lists of the identified systematic reviews
139	                           and meta-analyses were manually searched to identify potential eligible studies. Article
140	                           screening and selection were independently conducted by two authors (Y.W. and W.S.).
141	
142	                           2.3. Eligibility Criteria
143	                                The inclusion criteria were established based on the Population, Intervention, Compar-

145	                           administration of acute, rather than long-term, caffeine interventions; (3) Comparison:

157	                           2.4. Data Extraction
158	                                 Data extraction was independently conducted by two authors (Y.W. and W.S.) using
159	                           a predefined template. The extracted information included: (1) study characteristics
160	                           (first author, publication year, country); (2) subject characteristics (age, sex, sample size);
161	                           (3) intervention characteristics (caffeine dosage and timing); and (4) outcome characteristics
162	                           (exercise modality, PPO, fastest sprint time).

164	                           2.5. Methodological Quality Assessment
165	                                The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane
166	                           risk of bias tool [1,32] and further evaluated with the Physiotherapy Evidence Database
167	                           (PEDro) scale. The Cochrane risk of bias tool evaluates five domains of potential bias,
168	                           including selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, and reporting
169	                           bias. Each domain rated as having a low, unclear, or high risk of bias. The PEDro scale
170	                           comprises 11 items, and studies scoring <4 points, 4–5 points, 6–8 points, and ≥9 points
171	                           were categorized as poor, average, good, and excellent quality, respectively [33].

177	                                The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)

179	                           egorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. The GRADE assessment was conducted

182	                           2.7. Statistical Analysis
183	                                 From each included study, the mean and standard deviation (SD) of RSA-related
184	                           variables were extracted for both caffeine and placebo conditions. Data were pooled using
185	                           fixed-effects models to obtain the weighted mean difference (WMD) and 95% confidence
186	                           intervals (CIs). When studies reported standard errors (SEs) and 95% CIs instead of SDs,
187	                           the corresponding SD was estimated [34,35].
188	                                 Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic, in cases of substantial heterogeneity,
189	                           subgroup analysis and sensitivity analysis were conducted to explore potential sources of
190	                           variation [36,37]. Subgroup analyses examined the influence of (1) caffeine dosage (<6 vs.
191	                           ≥6 mg/kg BW), (2) exercise modality (cycling vs. running), and (3) participant sex (male
192	                           vs. female).
193	                                 Forest plots were generated using RevMan software (Version 5.4), while sensitivity
194	                           analysis, funnel plot, and meta-regression were performed using Stata software (Version
195	                           15.0). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

359	                           4. Discussion
360	                           4.1. Main Findings
361	                                The primary objective of this study was to systematically synthesize and quantify
362	                           the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA across diverse study populations, exercise
363	                           modalities, and caffeine dosages. A total of 13 studies were included in the final analysis,
364	                           and the pooled results revealed that acute caffeine ingestion exerted a statistically signif-
365	                           icant ergogenic effect on RSA in both male and female participants. Subgroup analyses
366	                           further indicated that this performance-enhancing effect was consistent across two common
367	                           exercise modalities—cycling and running. Notably, a dosage-dependent response was
368	                           observed, with caffeine ingestion at a dose of ≥6 mg/kg BW yielding a more pronounced
369	                           ergogenic impact on RSA compared to lower doses.
370	
371	                           4.2. Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability
372	                                The findings of the present study demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion signifi-
373	                           cantly improved RSA, which is congruent with the results of prior studies [27,29]. Beyond
374	                           oral ingestion, alternative routes of caffeine administration have also been explored for
375	                           their effects on anaerobic performance. For instance, caffeine mouth rinse (without swal-
376	                           lowing) has been shown to enhance maximal power production during short-duration,
377	                           high-intensity exercise. This effect is thought to be mediated by caffeine’s activation of oral
378	                           cavity adenosine receptors, which transmit sensory signals to the central nervous system to
379	                           augment motor unit recruitment, a mechanism that may also contribute to improvements
380	                           in RSA, given the sport-specific demand for repeated maximal power outputs [46].
381	                                Previous research has posited that ergogenic efficacy of caffeine may be attenuated
382	                           under conditions of cumulative fatigue, a physiological challenge inherently associated
383	                           with RSA protocols [38]. Mechanistically, caffeine exerts its central and peripheral effects
384	                           primarily as a non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist, specifically targeting A1 and
385	                           A2A receptors [1]. By competitively binding to these receptors, caffeine inhibits the action
386	                           of adenosine, a key neuromodulator of fatigue, sleep, and arousal, thereby delaying the
387	                           onset of perceived fatigue and enhancing central drive [47]. It is important to distinguish
388	                           between caffeine’s effects on alertness and its capacity to reverse physiological fatigue:
389	                           while caffeine has been shown to transiently improve subjective ratings of alertness in
390	                           sleep-deprived individuals, it cannot mitigate the underlying physiological deficits (e.g.,
391	                           reduced glycogen stores, impaired neuromuscular function) induced by prolonged sleep
392	                           deprivation [48]. Extending this to exercise contexts, caffeine ingestion has been shown to
393	                           reduce time to exhaustion during endurance exercise; however, this effect was attributed to
394	                           improvements in mood and perceived exertion rather than a direct attenuation of neuro-
395	                           muscular fatigue [49]. Consistent with these findings, further research has indicated that
396	                           the efficacy of caffeine in enhance RSA diminishes as exercise-induced fatigue accumulates
397	                           over successive sprints [50]. To address this potential attenuation and ensure sensitivity to
398	                           caffeine’s true ergogenic potential, the present study focused on two key RSA outcomes:
399	                           PPO (a measure of maximal anaerobic capacity) and fastest sprint time (a marker of optimal
400	                           sprint performance) rather than MPO and mean sprint time, which are more susceptible to
401	                           the confounding effects of cumulative fatigue.
402	                                A critical methodological consideration in caffeine research is the timing of RSA assess-
403	                           ment relative to ingestion, as plasma caffeine concentration reaches its peak approximately
404	                           60 min post-ingestion in healthy adults [51]. To minimize variability in caffeine bioavailabil-
405	                           ity across studies, all 13 included investigations consistently administered caffeine 60 min
406	                           prior to RSA testing, a methodological consistency that strengthens the internal validity of
407	                           the present meta-analysis.

412	                           4.3. Effects of Caffeine Dosage on Repeated Sprint Ability
413	                                 Caffeine dosage is a critical moderator of its ergogenic effect on RSA, and the present
414	                           subgroup analysis confirmed a dose–response relationship. Specifically, acute caffeine
415	                           ingestion at a dose of ≥6 mg/kg BW (high-dose) significantly enhanced RSA, while acute
416	                           caffeine ingestion of <6 mg/kg BW (low-dose) did not elicit a statistically significant effect.
417	                           This observation aligns with previous studies that high-dose caffeine confers a robust
418	                           ergogenic benefit for RSA [23,52]. Interestingly, existing literature suggests that doses
419	                           exceeding 6 mg/kg BW (e.g., 9 mg/kg BW) do not further amplify RSA improvements;
420	                           studies comparing 6 mg/kg BW and 9 mg/kg BW have found no significant differences
421	                           in RSA outcomes, indicating a potential ceiling effect for caffeine’s ergogenic action on
422	                           repeated sprints [23,52].
423	                                 A notable discrepancy emerged between the present findings and a study by Wang
424	                           et al. [24], which reported that low-dose (rather than high-dose) caffeine improved RSA.
425	                           This inconsistency may be attributed to the unique characteristics of the participant sample
426	                           in Wang et al.’s study: the authors recruited individuals with low habitual caffeine con-
427	                           sumption (defined as <60 mg/day). This may Population-based research has established
428	                           that habitual caffeine intake modulates sensitivity to acute caffeine ingestion—low con-
429	                           sumers typically exhibit greater physiological and performance responses to lower doses,
430	                           whereas high consumers may develop tolerance, requiring higher doses to achieve similar
431	                           effects [53]. Thus, the low habitual intake of Wang et al.’s participants likely enhanced their
432	                           responsiveness to low-dose caffeine, accounting for the divergent results.
433	
434	                           4.4. Effects of Exercise Modality on Repeated Sprint Ability
435	                                Cycling and running are the two most prevalent exercise modalities used to assess RSA
436	                           in experimental research, as they allow for precise measurement of power output (cycling)
437	                           and sprint time (running) while controlling for external variables (e.g., terrain, technique).
438	                           The present subgroup analysis confirmed that acute caffeine ingestion improved RSA
439	                           across both modalities, with running-based RSA exhibiting a more pronounced effect, a
440	                           finding that is supported by multiple previous studies [46,54,55]. In cycling-based RSA
441	                           protocols, Schneiker et al. [54] reported that participants who ingested caffeine (6 mg/kg
442	                           BW) exhibited significantly higher PPO across repeated sprints compared to those in the
443	                           placebo group, a result that was later replicated by Beaven et al. [46], who observed a
444	                           significant increase in PPO following caffeine ingestion in trained males. In running-based
445	                           RSA tests, Glaister et al. [55] demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion (5 mg/kg BW)
446	                           significantly reduced fastest sprint time in physically active males.
447	                                An important practical consideration is the ecological validity of exercise modalities
448	                           for specific sports. Running-based RSA tests entail greater total energy expenditure and
449	                           neuromuscular demand (e.g., activation of lower-body muscles, balance control) compared
450	                           to cycling tests, which are constrained by fixed pedaling mechanics [56]. This difference
451	                           suggests that cycling may not be the optimal modality for assessing RSA in running-based
452	                           sports (e.g., basketball, volleyball, soccer), as it fails to replicate the movement patterns and
453	                           physiological stressors inherent to these sports. This potential lack of ecological validity
454	                           may explain why some studies utilizing cycling tests to assess RSA in running-based sports
455	                           athletes found no significant effect of acute caffeine ingestion on PPO [57,58]. These findings
456	                           highlight the importance of selecting exercise modalities that align with the sport-specific
457	                           demands of the participant population when investigating caffeine’s effects on RSA.
458	
459	                           4.5. Effects of Participant Sex on Repeated Sprint Ability
460	                               While the present meta-analysis confirmed that acute caffeine ingestion significantly
461	                           improved RSA in both males and females, subgroup analysis and a synthesis of existing

466	                           literature revealed substantial heterogeneous in the magnitude and consistency of this
467	                           effect across sexes.
468	                                 In the male group, the pooled results indicated a significant ergogenic effect of caffeine
469	                           on RSA; however, this finding contrasts with a study by Kopec et al. [59], which reported no
470	                           differences in RSA between caffeine (6 mg/kg BW) and placebo groups in male team-sport
471	                           athletes. The discrepancy may be attributed to the low sample size (n = 11) and moderate
472	                           training status of participants in Kopec et al.’s study, which may have reduced statistical
473	                           power to detect small-to-moderate effect sizes. In the female subgroup, our findings align
474	                           with previous studies [23,60]. Bougrine et al. [23] demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion
475	                           at 6 mg/kg BW significantly improved RSA in female team-sport athletes, while another
476	                           study by Lara et al. [60] reported that even a low dose of caffeine (3 mg/kg BW) enhanced
477	                           RSA in female soccer players. Conversely, a previous meta-analysis by Gomez-Bruton
478	                           et al. [26] found no significant effect of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA in female team-sport
479	                           athletes. This null finding may be attributable to methodological heterogeneity, particularly
480	                           the restriction of their analytical sample to participants aged ≥ 18 years, thereby limiting
481	                           direct comparability with investigations incorporating younger cohorts.
482	                                 A key physiological mechanism underlying potential sex differences in caffeine re-
483	                           sponsiveness is the rate of caffeine metabolism. Females have been shown to metabolize
484	                           caffeine more slowly than males, primarily due to the inhibitory effect of estrogen on
485	                           CYP1A2, the primary hepatic enzyme responsible for caffeine degradation [61]. This slower
486	                           metabolism results in prolonged plasma caffeine concentrations in females, which may
487	                           alter the timing and magnitude of caffeine’s ergogenic effect on RSA. Pérez-López et al. [39]
488	                           provided empirical support for this mechanism, reporting that following acute caffeine
489	                           ingestion, males exhibited higher PPO in the first two sprints of an RSA protocol, whereas
490	                           females demonstrated superior PPO in the final two sprints. This temporal difference
491	                           likely reflects the prolonged caffeine availability in females, which mitigates fatigue during
492	                           later sprints.
493	                                 Given the equivocal nature of existing evidence, with some studies reporting sex-
494	                           specific effects and others finding no differences, further research is warranted to explicitly
495	                           investigate sex as a moderator of caffeine’s effects on RSA. Future studies should control for
496	                           variables such as menstrual cycle phase (in females), habitual caffeine intake, and training
497	                           status to reduce heterogeneity and clarify the role of sex.
498	
499	                           4.6. Practical Implications
500	                                These findings have practical implications for athletes and coaches seeking to opti-
501	                           mize RSA performance: acute caffeine ingestion at 6 mg/kg BW, administered 60 min
502	                           pre-exercise, represents an evidence-based strategy to enhance repeated sprint outcomes.
503	                           Future research should address the limitations of the present study by explicitly investi-
504	                           gating the moderating effects of training status, habitual caffeine intake, and participant
505	                           age on caffeine’s ergogenic effect on RSA. Additionally, studies utilizing sport-specific
506	                           RSA protocols (e.g., soccer-specific running drills, basketball agility sprints) are needed
507	                           to further enhance the ecological validity and translational utility of caffeine research in
508	                           applied sports settings.
509	
510	                           4.7. Limitations
511	                                This study has several limitations. First, previous studies have employed diverse
512	                           forms of caffeine administration (e.g., powder, capsules, mouth rinse, caffeinated beverages)
513	                           [39,41,62,63]. Due to the limited number of eligible studies, the present analysis included
514	                           only powder and capsule forms without distinguishing their effects separately. Second,
515	                           substantial variability in the athletic capabilities of participants may have influenced

520	                           RSA outcomes following acute caffeine ingestion. Differences in training status, habitual
521	                           caffeine use, and sport-specific demands can substantially modulate the ergogenic response
522	                           to caffeine [64,65]. As previously noted, cycling may not represent the most appropriate
523	                           testing modality for RSA in running-based sports [56]. Therefore, future research should
524	                           further delineate the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA across various sport types
525	                           and performance contexts.
526	                                Finally, although several studies have reported adverse effects associated with acute
527	                           caffeine ingestion (e.g., such as ventricular fibrillation, irritability, and nervousness) [23,66],
528	                           these outcomes were not analyzed in the current study. For example, Bougrine et al. [23]
529	                           observed a higher incidence of side effects following caffeine ingestion at a dose of 9 mg/kg
530	                           BW. Consequently, future investigations should consider not only the ergogenic potential
531	                           but also the safety profile of different caffeine dosages to optimize performance benefits
532	                           while minimizing potential risks. In line with recommendations from the International
533	                           Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), caffeine doses of 3–6 mg/kg BW can enhance exercise
534	                           performance, whereas doses of 9 mg/kg are associated with a higher incidence of adverse
535	                           effects [15].

537	                           5. Conclusions
538	                                 The present systematic review and meta-analysis provide robust evidence that acute
539	                           caffeine ingestion (administered 60 min prior to exercise) exerts a significant ergogenic
540	                           effect on RSA in healthy adults. This effect is consistent across both male and female
541	                           participants, with no statistically significant sex difference observed in the pooled analysis.
542	                           Furthermore, acute caffeine ingestion enhances RSA in both cycling and running exercise
543	                           modalities, though the ecological validity of cycling for running-based sports should be
544	                           considered when interpreting these results. Moreover, caffeine ingestion at ≥6 mg/kg BW
545	                           yields a more pronounced ergogenic impact on RSA, whereas doses < 6 mg/kg BW do not
546	                           elicit significant performance improvements.
