                                                Caffeine, the primary bioactive compound found in widely consumed beverages such
(https://creativecommons.org/              as coffee, tea, and cocoa, acts as a central nervous system stimulant and adenosine receptor
licenses/by/4.0/).                         antagonist [1]. It is rapidly absorbed and exerts diverse physiological effects, including


Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                          https://doi.org/10.3390/nu17213475
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                              2 of 17



                           reducing fatigue, enhancing lipolysis, and increasing alertness [2–4]. Although generally
                           considered safe at typical consumption levels, excessive intake may cause adverse effects
                           such as anxiety, insomnia, and gastrointestinal discomfort [5–7]. Owing to its pronounced
                           physiological actions, caffeine has long been a subject of extensive research in the context
                           of performance enhancement and remains one of the most widely used legal psychoactive
                           substances worldwide.
                                 In the field of sports science, caffeine is recognized as a potent ergogenic aid capable
                           of augmenting athletic performance through multiple mechanisms. Early studies demon-
                           strated that caffeine enhances aerobic endurance primarily by promoting fat oxidation
                           and conserving muscle glycogen stores [8,9]. Subsequent research extended these observa-
                           tions, indicating that caffeine may also improve anaerobic endurance and high-intensity
                           exercise performance through multiple mechanisms, including reduced pain perception,
                           enhanced muscle contractility, and improved neural drive [10,11]. Notably, caffeine was
                           only removed from the World Anti-Doping Agency’s list of prohibited substances in 2004,
                           thereby legitimizing its use as an ergogenic aid among elite athletes. Since then, caffeine-
                           containing energy drinks have emerged as a popular vehicle for delivering this ergogenic
                           aid. These beverages typically combine substantial amounts of caffeine with additional
                           ingredients such as carbohydrates, B vitamins, and taurine, thereby providing an auxil-
                           iary energy source during exercise [12,13]. However, the primary ergogenic benefits are
                           largely attributed to their high caffeine content, with nearly half of professional athletes
                           reportedly using caffeine-based supplements to enhance performance [14]. According to
                           the International Society of Sports Nutrition, caffeine consumption approximately 60 min
                           prior to exercise can effectively improve various aspects of athletic performance, including
                           endurance capacity, high-intensity effort, and muscular strength [15].
                                 Repeated sprint ability (RSA) is a performance parameter that depends primarily on
                           the adenosine triphosphate-creatine phosphate (ATP-CP) energy system and plays a crucial
                           role in high-intensity intermittent sports such as basketball, soccer, and rugby [16–19].
                           However, the ergogenic potential of acute caffeine ingestion for improving RSA remains
                           controversial. Several studies have reported that acute caffeine supplementation enhances
                           RSA by increasing both peak power output (PPO) and mean power output (MPO) [20,21].
                           In contrast, other studies have failed to detect such benefits. For instance, Bernardo et al. [22]
                           observed no significant differences in PPO or MPO between caffeine and placebo conditions
                           in male participants. Similarly, Houda et al. [23] reported that an acute caffeine dose of
                           3 mg/kg body weight (BW) did not significantly influence RSA in young female athletes,
                           whereas higher doses of 6 or 9 mg/kg BW improved performance by reducing both the
                           fastest and mean sprint time, suggesting a potential dose–response effect. Conversely,
                           another research demonstrated that even a 3 mg/kg BW caffeine dose was sufficient to
                           enhance both PPO and MPO during repeated sprints [24]. Collectively, these inconsistent
                           findings indicate that the ergogenic effects of caffeine on RSA remain equivocal and may
                           be influenced by interindividual differences in caffeine sensitivity [25].
                                 Existing meta-analyses examining the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA have
                           also produced divergent conclusions. For instance, Gomez-Bruton et al. [26] reported no
                           significant effect of caffeine on RSA in females athletes, whereas López-Torres et al. [27]
                           demonstrated a positive ergogenic effect. Similarly, Lopes-Silva et al. [28] found that acute
                           caffeine ingestion did not significantly improve RSA, while another meta-analysis revealed
                           that caffeine markedly enhanced high-intensity performance in elite athletes during both
                           real or simulated competitions [29]. These discrepancies among meta-analytic findings may
                           stem from methodological limitations, such as the inclusion of only female participants, the
                           absence of dosage stratification, and inadequate control for habitual caffeine consumption.
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                            3 of 17



                                Therefore, to address these inconsistencies and methodological gaps, the present
                           systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate the effects of
                           acute caffeine ingestion on RSA.

                           2. Materials and Methods
                           2.1. Design
                                This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the
                           Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluation and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guide-
                           lines [30]. The study protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective
                           Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD420251150247).

                           2.2. Search Strategy
                                A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane
                           Library, Web of science, and Scopus databases from their inception to 6 September 2025.
                           The search strategy employed the keywords and MESH terms “caffeine” and “repeated
                           sprint ability” (Table S1). Additionally, reference lists of the identified systematic reviews
                           and meta-analyses were manually searched to identify potential eligible studies. Article
                           screening and selection were independently conducted by two authors (Y.W. and W.S.).

                           2.3. Eligibility Criteria
                                The inclusion criteria were established based on the Population, Intervention, Compar-
                           ison, and Outcome (PICO) principle: (1) Population: human participants; (2) Intervention:
                           administration of acute, rather than long-term, caffeine interventions; (3) Comparison:
                           evaluation of acute effects between caffeine ingestion and placebo control groups; and
                           (4) Outcome: the primary endpoint was PPO.
                                PPO was assessed using cycle ergometer, while fastest sprint time was measured
                           during running-based tests. Where necessary, fastest sprint time data were converted to
                           PPO using the following equation [31]:

                                            Power output = (body mass (kg) × distance (m)2 )/time (s)3                 (1)

                                 Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) non-English publications; (2) conference papers;
                           (3) review articles; and (4) animal or in vitro studies.

                           2.4. Data Extraction
                                 Data extraction was independently conducted by two authors (Y.W. and W.S.) using
                           a predefined template. The extracted information included: (1) study characteristics
                           (first author, publication year, country); (2) subject characteristics (age, sex, sample size);
                           (3) intervention characteristics (caffeine dosage and timing); and (4) outcome characteristics
                           (exercise modality, PPO, fastest sprint time).

                           2.5. Methodological Quality Assessment
                                The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane
                           risk of bias tool [1,32] and further evaluated with the Physiotherapy Evidence Database
                           (PEDro) scale. The Cochrane risk of bias tool evaluates five domains of potential bias,
                           including selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, and reporting
                           bias. Each domain rated as having a low, unclear, or high risk of bias. The PEDro scale
                           comprises 11 items, and studies scoring <4 points, 4–5 points, 6–8 points, and ≥9 points
                           were categorized as poor, average, good, and excellent quality, respectively [33].
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                            4 of 17



                           2.6. Certainty Assessment
                                The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)
                           approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence across outcomes, with ratings cat-
                           egorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. The GRADE assessment was conducted
                           two independent authors (Y.W. and W.S.).

                           2.7. Statistical Analysis
                                 From each included study, the mean and standard deviation (SD) of RSA-related
                           variables were extracted for both caffeine and placebo conditions. Data were pooled using
                           fixed-effects models to obtain the weighted mean difference (WMD) and 95% confidence
                           intervals (CIs). When studies reported standard errors (SEs) and 95% CIs instead of SDs,
                           the corresponding SD was estimated [34,35].
                                 Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic, in cases of substantial heterogeneity,
                           subgroup analysis and sensitivity analysis were conducted to explore potential sources of
                           variation [36,37]. Subgroup analyses examined the influence of (1) caffeine dosage (<6 vs.
                           ≥6 mg/kg BW), (2) exercise modality (cycling vs. running), and (3) participant sex (male
                           vs. female).
                                 Forest plots were generated using RevMan software (Version 5.4), while sensitivity
                           analysis, funnel plot, and meta-regression were performed using Stata software (Version
                           15.0). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

                           3. Results
                           3.1. Studies Selection
                                 As illustrated in Figure 1, the initial database search identified 844 records. After
                           removing duplicates, 507 studies remained for title and abstract screening. Following this
                           process, 25 potentially eligible studies were retained for full-text evaluation. Upon detailed
                           review, 12 studies were excluded for the following reasons: (1) experimental design (n = 6);
                           (2) caffeine ingestion was combined with other interventions (n = 5); (3) absence of relevant
                           outcome indicators (n = 1). Finally, 13 studies [10–14,29–36] met the inclusion criteria.




                           Figure 1. PRISMA flowchart of study selection.

                           3.2. Characteristics of the Included Studies
                                 The characteristics of the included studies and participants are summarized in Table 1.
                           Among the 13 studies, 2 studies [38,39] employed a low caffeine dosage (<6 mg/kg BW),
                           7 studies [21,22,40–44] used a high caffeine dosage (≥6 mg/kg BW), and 4 studies [20,
                           23,24,45] examined both low and high dosages. Regarding participant characteristics,
                           six studies [21,22,24,38,42,44] involved only males, 6 studies [20,23,40,41,43,45] included
                           only females, and 1 study [39] involved participants of both sexes. Eight studies [21,22,24,38,
                           39,42,43,45] reported PPO data assessed via cycling tests, whereas 5 studies [20,23,40,41,44]
                           provided data for fastest sprint time measured using running tests. Caffeine dosage ranged
                           from 3 to 9 mg/kg BW, with ingestion typically occurring 60 min prior to testing.

                           3.3. Risk of Bias
                                The risk of bias assessment using the Cochrane risk of bias tool identified two studies
                           as having a high risk of reporting bias, while the remaining studies were generally classified
                           as low risk across the domains of selection, performance, detection, attrition, and reporting
                           biases (Figure S1). Based on the PEDro scale, 13 studies [20–24,38–45] were rated as excellent
                           quality (Table S2).

                           3.4. Meta-Analysis
                                 Compared with placebo, acute caffeine ingestion significantly enhanced RSA (WMD,
                           5.28, 95% CI, 2.49 to 8.07, p = 0.0002, I2 = 7%, Figure 2).




                           Figure 2. Meta-analysis results of the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA [20–24,38–45]. Articles
                           by the same author are distinguished by the suffixes “a” and “b”. Morning and evening sessions are
                           denoted by “m” and “e”, respectively; participant sex by “M” (male) and “F” (female); caffeine dose
                           by “3”, “6”, or “9” (mg/kg body weight); and inter-interval rest duration by “20” or “90” (min).

                           3.5. Subgroup Analysis
                           3.5.1. Caffeine Dosage
                                 When stratified by caffeine dosage, 9 studies investigated low doses (<6 mg/kg BW),
                           including 7 studies using 3 mg/kg BW and 2 studies using 5 mg/kg BW. No significant
                           improvements in RSA were observed within this subgroup (WMD, 2.16, 95% CI, −2.87 to
                           7.19, p = 0.40, I2 = 0%, Figure 3). In contrast, 15 studies assessed high doses, with 13 studies
                           using 6 mg/kg BW and 2 studies using 9 mg/kg BW. In this subgroup, caffeine ingestion
                           produced a significant improvement in RSA (WMD, 6.67, 95% CI, 3.32 to 10.02, p < 0.0001,
                           I2 = 23%, Figure 3).

                           3.5.2. Exercise Modality
                                When stratified by exercise modality, 14 studies employed cycling protocols and
                           10 studies used running-based tests. Significant improvements in RSA were observed for
                           both modalities (cycling: WMD, 8.77, 95% CI, 1.98 to 15.56, p = 0.01, I2 = 5%; running:
                           WMD, 4.56, 95% CI, 1.58 to 7.55, p = 0.003, I2 = 9%, Figure 4), with running-based RSA
                           exhibiting a more pronounced effect.

                           3.5.3. Participant Sex
                                Subgroup analyses by participant sex revealed that caffeine ingestion significantly
                           enhanced RSA in both male and female (male: WMD, 13.11, 95% CI, 5.63 to 20.59, p = 0.0006,
                           I2 = 29%; female: WMD, 4.03, 95% CI, 1.10 to 6.97, p = 0.007, I2 = 0%, Figure 5), with male
                           participants exhibiting a more pronounced effect.




                           Figure 5. Meta-analysis results of the effects of participant sex on RSA [20–24,38–45]. Articles by
                           the same author are distinguished by the suffixes “a” and “b”. Morning and evening sessions are
                           denoted by “m” and “e”, respectively; participant sex by “M” (male) and “F” (female); caffeine dose
                           by “3”, “6”, or “9” (mg/kg body weight); and inter-interval rest duration by “20” or “90” (min).

                           3.6. Publication Bias
                               Possible publication bias was assessed using funnel plot analysis (Figure S2). Visual
                           inspection indicated a substantial asymmetry, suggesting a likelihood of publication bias.
                           However, application of the Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill method did not alter the
                           overall effect size, confirming the robustness of the pooled estimates. This finding was
                           supported by Egger’s test (p = 0.328, Table S3).

                           3.7. Sensitivity Analysis
                                Sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the overall effect of acute caffeine ingestion
                           on RSA remained stable in both magnitude and direction after sequential exclusion of
                           individual studies (Figure S3). These results confirm the robustness and reliability of the
                           meta-analytic findings.

                           3.8. GRADE Summary
                                The certainty of the evidence underpinning our findings was systematically assessed
                           using the GRADE framework. Following this rigorous appraisal, the overall certainty
                           of the evidence was rated as high, indicating strong confidence in the reliability and
                           generalizability of our conclusions (Table S4).
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                           10 of 17



                           4. Discussion
                           4.1. Main Findings
                                The primary objective of this study was to systematically synthesize and quantify
                           the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA across diverse study populations, exercise
                           modalities, and caffeine dosages. A total of 13 studies were included in the final analysis,
                           and the pooled results revealed that acute caffeine ingestion exerted a statistically signif-
                           icant ergogenic effect on RSA in both male and female participants. Subgroup analyses
                           further indicated that this performance-enhancing effect was consistent across two common
                           exercise modalities—cycling and running. Notably, a dosage-dependent response was
                           observed, with caffeine ingestion at a dose of ≥6 mg/kg BW yielding a more pronounced
                           ergogenic impact on RSA compared to lower doses.

                           4.2. Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability
                                The findings of the present study demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion signifi-
                           cantly improved RSA, which is congruent with the results of prior studies [27,29]. Beyond
                           oral ingestion, alternative routes of caffeine administration have also been explored for
                           their effects on anaerobic performance. For instance, caffeine mouth rinse (without swal-
                           lowing) has been shown to enhance maximal power production during short-duration,
                           high-intensity exercise. This effect is thought to be mediated by caffeine’s activation of oral
                           cavity adenosine receptors, which transmit sensory signals to the central nervous system to
                           augment motor unit recruitment, a mechanism that may also contribute to improvements
                           in RSA, given the sport-specific demand for repeated maximal power outputs [46].
                                Previous research has posited that ergogenic efficacy of caffeine may be attenuated
                           under conditions of cumulative fatigue, a physiological challenge inherently associated
                           with RSA protocols [38]. Mechanistically, caffeine exerts its central and peripheral effects
                           primarily as a non-selective adenosine receptor antagonist, specifically targeting A1 and
                           A2A receptors [1]. By competitively binding to these receptors, caffeine inhibits the action
                           of adenosine, a key neuromodulator of fatigue, sleep, and arousal, thereby delaying the
                           onset of perceived fatigue and enhancing central drive [47]. It is important to distinguish
                           between caffeine’s effects on alertness and its capacity to reverse physiological fatigue:
                           while caffeine has been shown to transiently improve subjective ratings of alertness in
                           sleep-deprived individuals, it cannot mitigate the underlying physiological deficits (e.g.,
                           reduced glycogen stores, impaired neuromuscular function) induced by prolonged sleep
                           deprivation [48]. Extending this to exercise contexts, caffeine ingestion has been shown to
                           reduce time to exhaustion during endurance exercise; however, this effect was attributed to
                           improvements in mood and perceived exertion rather than a direct attenuation of neuro-
                           muscular fatigue [49]. Consistent with these findings, further research has indicated that
                           the efficacy of caffeine in enhance RSA diminishes as exercise-induced fatigue accumulates
                           over successive sprints [50]. To address this potential attenuation and ensure sensitivity to
                           caffeine’s true ergogenic potential, the present study focused on two key RSA outcomes:
                           PPO (a measure of maximal anaerobic capacity) and fastest sprint time (a marker of optimal
                           sprint performance) rather than MPO and mean sprint time, which are more susceptible to
                           the confounding effects of cumulative fatigue.
                                A critical methodological consideration in caffeine research is the timing of RSA assess-
                           ment relative to ingestion, as plasma caffeine concentration reaches its peak approximately
                           60 min post-ingestion in healthy adults [51]. To minimize variability in caffeine bioavailabil-
                           ity across studies, all 13 included investigations consistently administered caffeine 60 min
                           prior to RSA testing, a methodological consistency that strengthens the internal validity of
                           the present meta-analysis.
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                             11 of 17



                           4.3. Effects of Caffeine Dosage on Repeated Sprint Ability
                                 Caffeine dosage is a critical moderator of its ergogenic effect on RSA, and the present
                           subgroup analysis confirmed a dose–response relationship. Specifically, acute caffeine
                           ingestion at a dose of ≥6 mg/kg BW (high-dose) significantly enhanced RSA, while acute
                           caffeine ingestion of <6 mg/kg BW (low-dose) did not elicit a statistically significant effect.
                           This observation aligns with previous studies that high-dose caffeine confers a robust
                           ergogenic benefit for RSA [23,52]. Interestingly, existing literature suggests that doses
                           exceeding 6 mg/kg BW (e.g., 9 mg/kg BW) do not further amplify RSA improvements;
                           studies comparing 6 mg/kg BW and 9 mg/kg BW have found no significant differences
                           in RSA outcomes, indicating a potential ceiling effect for caffeine’s ergogenic action on
                           repeated sprints [23,52].
                                 A notable discrepancy emerged between the present findings and a study by Wang
                           et al. [24], which reported that low-dose (rather than high-dose) caffeine improved RSA.
                           This inconsistency may be attributed to the unique characteristics of the participant sample
                           in Wang et al.’s study: the authors recruited individuals with low habitual caffeine con-
                           sumption (defined as <60 mg/day). This may Population-based research has established
                           that habitual caffeine intake modulates sensitivity to acute caffeine ingestion—low con-
                           sumers typically exhibit greater physiological and performance responses to lower doses,
                           whereas high consumers may develop tolerance, requiring higher doses to achieve similar
                           effects [53]. Thus, the low habitual intake of Wang et al.’s participants likely enhanced their
                           responsiveness to low-dose caffeine, accounting for the divergent results.

                           4.4. Effects of Exercise Modality on Repeated Sprint Ability
                                Cycling and running are the two most prevalent exercise modalities used to assess RSA
                           in experimental research, as they allow for precise measurement of power output (cycling)
                           and sprint time (running) while controlling for external variables (e.g., terrain, technique).
                           The present subgroup analysis confirmed that acute caffeine ingestion improved RSA
                           across both modalities, with running-based RSA exhibiting a more pronounced effect, a
                           finding that is supported by multiple previous studies [46,54,55]. In cycling-based RSA
                           protocols, Schneiker et al. [54] reported that participants who ingested caffeine (6 mg/kg
                           BW) exhibited significantly higher PPO across repeated sprints compared to those in the
                           placebo group, a result that was later replicated by Beaven et al. [46], who observed a
                           significant increase in PPO following caffeine ingestion in trained males. In running-based
                           RSA tests, Glaister et al. [55] demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion (5 mg/kg BW)
                           significantly reduced fastest sprint time in physically active males.
                                An important practical consideration is the ecological validity of exercise modalities
                           for specific sports. Running-based RSA tests entail greater total energy expenditure and
                           neuromuscular demand (e.g., activation of lower-body muscles, balance control) compared
                           to cycling tests, which are constrained by fixed pedaling mechanics [56]. This difference
                           suggests that cycling may not be the optimal modality for assessing RSA in running-based
                           sports (e.g., basketball, volleyball, soccer), as it fails to replicate the movement patterns and
                           physiological stressors inherent to these sports. This potential lack of ecological validity
                           may explain why some studies utilizing cycling tests to assess RSA in running-based sports
                           athletes found no significant effect of acute caffeine ingestion on PPO [57,58]. These findings
                           highlight the importance of selecting exercise modalities that align with the sport-specific
                           demands of the participant population when investigating caffeine’s effects on RSA.

                           4.5. Effects of Participant Sex on Repeated Sprint Ability
                               While the present meta-analysis confirmed that acute caffeine ingestion significantly
                           improved RSA in both males and females, subgroup analysis and a synthesis of existing
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                            12 of 17



                           literature revealed substantial heterogeneous in the magnitude and consistency of this
                           effect across sexes.
                                 In the male group, the pooled results indicated a significant ergogenic effect of caffeine
                           on RSA; however, this finding contrasts with a study by Kopec et al. [59], which reported no
                           differences in RSA between caffeine (6 mg/kg BW) and placebo groups in male team-sport
                           athletes. The discrepancy may be attributed to the low sample size (n = 11) and moderate
                           training status of participants in Kopec et al.’s study, which may have reduced statistical
                           power to detect small-to-moderate effect sizes. In the female subgroup, our findings align
                           with previous studies [23,60]. Bougrine et al. [23] demonstrated that acute caffeine ingestion
                           at 6 mg/kg BW significantly improved RSA in female team-sport athletes, while another
                           study by Lara et al. [60] reported that even a low dose of caffeine (3 mg/kg BW) enhanced
                           RSA in female soccer players. Conversely, a previous meta-analysis by Gomez-Bruton
                           et al. [26] found no significant effect of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA in female team-sport
                           athletes. This null finding may be attributable to methodological heterogeneity, particularly
                           the restriction of their analytical sample to participants aged ≥ 18 years, thereby limiting
                           direct comparability with investigations incorporating younger cohorts.
                                 A key physiological mechanism underlying potential sex differences in caffeine re-
                           sponsiveness is the rate of caffeine metabolism. Females have been shown to metabolize
                           caffeine more slowly than males, primarily due to the inhibitory effect of estrogen on
                           CYP1A2, the primary hepatic enzyme responsible for caffeine degradation [61]. This slower
                           metabolism results in prolonged plasma caffeine concentrations in females, which may
                           alter the timing and magnitude of caffeine’s ergogenic effect on RSA. Pérez-López et al. [39]
                           provided empirical support for this mechanism, reporting that following acute caffeine
                           ingestion, males exhibited higher PPO in the first two sprints of an RSA protocol, whereas
                           females demonstrated superior PPO in the final two sprints. This temporal difference
                           likely reflects the prolonged caffeine availability in females, which mitigates fatigue during
                           later sprints.
                                 Given the equivocal nature of existing evidence, with some studies reporting sex-
                           specific effects and others finding no differences, further research is warranted to explicitly
                           investigate sex as a moderator of caffeine’s effects on RSA. Future studies should control for
                           variables such as menstrual cycle phase (in females), habitual caffeine intake, and training
                           status to reduce heterogeneity and clarify the role of sex.

                           4.6. Practical Implications
                                These findings have practical implications for athletes and coaches seeking to opti-
                           mize RSA performance: acute caffeine ingestion at 6 mg/kg BW, administered 60 min
                           pre-exercise, represents an evidence-based strategy to enhance repeated sprint outcomes.
                           Future research should address the limitations of the present study by explicitly investi-
                           gating the moderating effects of training status, habitual caffeine intake, and participant
                           age on caffeine’s ergogenic effect on RSA. Additionally, studies utilizing sport-specific
                           RSA protocols (e.g., soccer-specific running drills, basketball agility sprints) are needed
                           to further enhance the ecological validity and translational utility of caffeine research in
                           applied sports settings.

                           4.7. Limitations
                                This study has several limitations. First, previous studies have employed diverse
                           forms of caffeine administration (e.g., powder, capsules, mouth rinse, caffeinated beverages)
                           [39,41,62,63]. Due to the limited number of eligible studies, the present analysis included
                           only powder and capsule forms without distinguishing their effects separately. Second,
                           substantial variability in the athletic capabilities of participants may have influenced
 Nutrients 2025, 17, 3475                                                                                                     13 of 17



                           RSA outcomes following acute caffeine ingestion. Differences in training status, habitual
                           caffeine use, and sport-specific demands can substantially modulate the ergogenic response
                           to caffeine [64,65]. As previously noted, cycling may not represent the most appropriate
                           testing modality for RSA in running-based sports [56]. Therefore, future research should
                           further delineate the effects of acute caffeine ingestion on RSA across various sport types
                           and performance contexts.
                                Finally, although several studies have reported adverse effects associated with acute
                           caffeine ingestion (e.g., such as ventricular fibrillation, irritability, and nervousness) [23,66],
                           these outcomes were not analyzed in the current study. For example, Bougrine et al. [23]
                           observed a higher incidence of side effects following caffeine ingestion at a dose of 9 mg/kg
                           BW. Consequently, future investigations should consider not only the ergogenic potential
                           but also the safety profile of different caffeine dosages to optimize performance benefits
                           while minimizing potential risks. In line with recommendations from the International
                           Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), caffeine doses of 3–6 mg/kg BW can enhance exercise
                           performance, whereas doses of 9 mg/kg are associated with a higher incidence of adverse
                           effects [15].

                           5. Conclusions
                                 The present systematic review and meta-analysis provide robust evidence that acute
                           caffeine ingestion (administered 60 min prior to exercise) exerts a significant ergogenic
                           effect on RSA in healthy adults. This effect is consistent across both male and female
                           participants, with no statistically significant sex difference observed in the pooled analysis.
                           Furthermore, acute caffeine ingestion enhances RSA in both cycling and running exercise
                           modalities, though the ecological validity of cycling for running-based sports should be
                           considered when interpreting these results. Moreover, caffeine ingestion at ≥6 mg/kg BW
                           yields a more pronounced ergogenic impact on RSA, whereas doses < 6 mg/kg BW do not
                           elicit significant performance improvements.

{
 "id": "Q11",
 "sourceFile": "The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury - A Scoping Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review' matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.1186/s40798-026-01118-6 is printed in the page header.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of six databases searched on 1 May 2025 that included seven studies (five qualitative, two cross-sectional) covering 403 female football players after ACL injury, all of them soccer players apart from one rugby union and one touch football participant. Uncertainty, fear, lack of confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers to return to sport and physical activity, while confidence, motivation, strong social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Seven studies, no critical appraisal of study quality, and 380 of the 403 players come from two Swedish cross-sectional studies, while the qualitative studies contributed 2 to 9 women each. Six of seven studies were mixed-sex with roughly 10% female participants, and the mostly qualitative evidence cannot show causal links.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat these barriers and facilitators as measured predictors of return to sport, when they are perceived experiences from a few small, mostly qualitative soccer studies and the review does not show that changing them improves outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Meredith S, Farley JB, Hunt J, Dent E. The Role of Psychosocial Factors in Returning to Physical Activity and Sport Among Female Football Players After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2026;12:148.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-026-01118-6",
  "abstract": "Scoping review of seven studies on psychosocial factors and return to physical activity and sport in female football players (in practice, soccer players) after anterior cruciate ligament injury. Fear, uncertainty, low confidence and poor social support were perceived barriers, while confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity were perceived facilitators.",
  "tldr": "For female soccer players after an ACL injury, fear, uncertainty, low confidence and weak social support were reported as barriers to return, and confidence, motivation, social support and athletic identity as helpers. The authors suggest considering these alongside physical milestones, but the evidence is perceptual and from a small number of studies.",
  "methods": "Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, registered with the Open Science Framework on 14 April 2025. SCOPUS, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, PsycInfo and Embase were searched from inception on 1 May 2025 for original research on psychosocial factors and return to sport or physical activity in female players of any football code with a surgically or non-surgically managed ACL injury and a sample mean age of 18 or older. Two reviewers screened records, no quality appraisal was done, and findings were synthesized narratively into themes.",
  "findings": "Seven studies (403 female players aged 16 to 56; 222 returned to sport and 181 did not) were included, five qualitative and two cross-sectional. Fear was reported in five studies and lack of confidence in three as barriers linked to returning at a lower level or not returning; uncertainty and poor social support were also perceived barriers. Confidence in healthcare professionals, motivation, positive social support and strong athletic identity were perceived facilitators, and one cross-sectional study found players who returned had higher motivation (p < 0.001).",
  "limitations": "The review did not appraise study quality, did not distinguish sex from gender, and could not establish causal relationships because most included studies were qualitative. {
 "id": "Q12",
 "sourceFile": "Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials' matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.3389/fphys.2026.1792091 is printed in the header and citation box.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797; 12 BFRT, 8 eccentric, 3 isokinetic and 2 plyometric trials) of resistance training after primary ACL reconstruction in adults or adolescents, compared mainly with usual multimodal rehabilitation. Blood flow restriction training ranked first for quadriceps strength (SMD 0.40 vs usual rehabilitation, 95% CI 0.07-0.73) and quadriceps mass (SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53), both at moderate certainty. Eccentric training ranked first for quality of life (SMD 1.31, 95% CI 0.01-2.63; very low certainty), and isokinetic training ranked highest for knee function without any significant pairwise difference.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only the BFRT versus usual rehabilitation comparisons for quadriceps strength and mass reached moderate certainty; knee function and quality of life comparisons were all very low certainty, and isokinetic and plyometric nodes rest on 3 and 2 trials. Trial participants are post-surgery patients not described as athletes, and most outcomes were measured at the end of the intervention.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the SUCRA rankings as a hierarchy, when only BFRT versus usual rehabilitation for quadriceps strength and mass is moderately certain and the isokinetic and eccentric rankings rest on very low certainty evidence.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Chen J, Wu Y, Xu H, Ren Y, Yang R, Yao S, et al. Comparative effectiveness of resistance training modalities after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Front Physiol. 2026;17:1792091.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fphys.2026.1792091",
  "abstract": "Network meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials (n = 797) comparing resistance training modalities after primary ACL reconstruction on quadriceps strength, quadriceps mass, knee function and health-related quality of life, using SUCRA rankings and GRADE. BFRT had the most consistent benefit for quadriceps strength and mass versus usual rehabilitation.",
  "tldr": "Blood flow restriction training was the only modality with moderate certainty evidence of better quadriceps strength and mass than usual rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction. Rankings for knee function (isokinetic) and quality of life (eccentric) are very low certainty and should be treated as provisional.",
  "methods": "Searches of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science and Google Scholar to 30 September 2025 for English-language randomized trials in adults or adolescents after primary ACL reconstruction comparing modality-dominant resistance training with standard multimodal rehabilitation or with each other. Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of standardized mean differences with SUCRA rankings, RoB 2 risk of bias, design-by-treatment and node-splitting consistency checks, and GRADE for network comparisons; registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251182456).",
  "findings": "For quadriceps strength (18 trials, 693 participants) BFRT ranked first (SUCRA 81.7; SMD 0.40, 95% CI 0.07-0.73 vs usual rehabilitation), and for quadriceps mass (10 trials, 293 participants) BFRT ranked first (SUCRA 79.1; SMD 0.82, 95% CI 0.11-1.53), both moderate certainty. For knee function (10 trials, 339 participants) isokinetic training ranked highest (SUCRA 87.7) but no pairwise difference was significant. For quality of life (7 trials, 173 participants) eccentric training ranked first (SUCRA 87.4; SMD 1.31, 95% CI 0.01-2.63, p = 0.050), with very low certainty and substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 73.5%).",
  "limitations": "The network was uneven, with only 3 isokinetic and 2 plyometric trials, and knee function and quality of life comparisons were all rated very low certainty. Cuff pressures, loading schemes, outcome instruments, time since surgery and graft type varied or were inconsistently reported, and most outcomes were measured immediately after the intervention. Risk of bias was low in 14 trials and some concerns in 8.",
  "practicalImplications": "BFRT can be considered when the main goal is quadriceps strength or size recovery, since it beat usual rehabilitation at moderate certainty. Eccentric training for quality of life and isokinetic training for knee function are very low certainty signals, and the comparator was usual rehabilitation that often already included strengthening.",
  "athleteDev": "Rehabilitation and performance staff can use BFRT as a supported option for early quadriceps recovery after ACL reconstruction. The review does not test sport-specific performance outcomes such as sprinting, jumping or change of direction.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to rehabilitation after primary ACL reconstruction, where BFRT improved quadriceps strength and mass versus usual rehabilitation. The review does not measure time to return to sport, sport readiness or re-injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/screeningLimitations/findings/limitations: GRADE certainty omitted -> added moderate certainty only for BFRT vs CON (strength and mass) and very low for all knee function and QoL comparisons ('For knee function, all comparisons were rated as very low certainty ... For QoL, all comparisons were rated as very low certainty')",
   "paper.tldr/practicalImplications: presented eccentric training for quality of life as an outcome match -> hedged as provisional ('ET may be considered ... although this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the limited certainty of evidence'); added p = 0.050 and I2 73.5%",
   "evidenceSummary/findings: added trial counts by modality and per outcome (18/693, 10/339, 10/293, 7/173) and risk of bias (14 low, 8 some concerns)",
   "synthesisCaution: broadened from isokinetic only to all rankings beyond BFRT vs CON"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Eligibility: kept INCLUDE. Trials enrolled adults or adolescents after primary ACL reconstruction who are not described as athletes, but post-ACLR resistance rehabilitation is exercise and athlete-health evidence that the paper frames around return to pivoting sport, so exclusion reason (c) does not apply. Under the population rule the patients get Mixed / Unspecified (mean ages 15.7 to 41.7 years), not athlete tags such as Injured Athletes.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "id": "Q14",
 "sourceFile": "Role of video review for sport-related concussion identification - a systematic review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Role of video review for sport-related concussion identification: a systematic review' matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2024-109603 is printed in the running footer.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Sports Medicine & Injury", "Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "American Football", "Ice Hockey", "Rugby", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 29 studies (3,281 clinically diagnosed concussions; 26 in professional competition, 27 in male athletes only) on visible signs and injury mechanisms identified by video review. Six diagnostic accuracy studies (718 concussions) found most individual visible signs had sensitivity below 50% and specificity above 90%, except 'slow to get up' (sensitivity 80%, specificity 27%), and no visible sign was seen in 23.6% of concussions. The authors conclude expert video review can reliably identify visible signs but must be complemented by multimodal assessment.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only eight studies had low risk of bias, the review was not preregistered, and differing sign definitions make the summary sensitivity and specificity approximate. All diagnostic accuracy data come from male professional athletes; the only two studies with female athletes examined injury mechanism, and under-18 and Para athletes were not covered.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the absence of a visible sign on video as reassurance, when no sign was seen in about a quarter of diagnosed concussions and most signs missed more than half of cases.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Townsend DC, Saker A, Scandrett K, Green M, Brownlow M, Riley P, et al. Role of video review for sport-related concussion identification: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2025.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2024-109603",
  "abstract": "Systematic review of the frequency and diagnostic accuracy of visible signs of sport-related concussion identified through video review, and of the role of injury mechanism. Of 29 included studies, most visible signs showed low sensitivity and high specificity, and only two studies included female athletes.",
  "tldr": "Visible signs on video are useful prompts to remove and assess a player, but most miss more than half of concussions and about a quarter of concussions show no sign at all. Video review should support, not replace, a full multimodal sideline assessment.",
  "methods": "Systematic review following PRISMA for diagnostic test accuracy, not preregistered, searching MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library from 1 January 2001, with the search updated to June 2024. Peer-reviewed English studies using clinical diagnosis or a consensus definition of concussion as reference were included; risk of bias used QUADAS-2, and summary sensitivity and specificity per visible sign were estimated with bivariate random-effects models where data allowed.",
  "findings": "The most frequent signs were 'slow to get up' (37.6%) and 'motor incoordination' (26.7%), and no visible sign was seen in 23.6% of concussions. Summary sensitivity was low for most signs (for example lying motionless 0.20, motor incoordination 0.32, impact seizure 0.05) with high specificity (0.91 to 1.00), while 'slow to get up' had sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.27. Expert raters generally agreed more than novices, though expert kappa values ranged from 0.08 to 0.89, and high impact speed, direct head contact with a solid object and foul play increased the likelihood of a concussion diagnosis.",
  "limitations": "Only eight of 29 studies had low risk of bias, most were retrospective, and rater blinding was often unreported. Visible sign definitions varied, which introduces error into summary estimates, and the evidence comes mainly from male professional sport where multi-angle footage is available. The review was funded by the Premier League and several authors were Premier League employees or consultants.",
  "practicalImplications": "A visible sign on video is a reason to remove and assess the player, but its absence does not rule out concussion, and 'slow to get up' is sensitive but not specific. Expert reviewers and standard sign definitions improve reliability, and video should feed into a multimodal assessment rather than stand alone.",
  "athleteDev": "Cannot inform performance work. For medical staff using video, it supports trained reviewers and treating video as a prompt for clinical assessment rather than a decision tool.",
  "rtp": "Relevant to concussion identification and removal from play, not to return-to-play progression or clearance. A negative video review cannot rule out concussion, so it should not shortcut the clinical assessment."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary/findings: omitted the 'slow to get up' exception and the no-visible-sign rate -> added ('slow to get up with a summary sensitivity of 80% and a summary specificity of 27%'; 'no visible sign seen (23.6%)')",
   "screeningLimitations: added that the review was not preregistered ('The review was not preregistered prior to it being conducted') and that all accuracy data are from male athletes ('27 focused exclusively on male athletes, one on female athletes and one compared both sexes'; the two female studies were mechanism-of-injury studies)",
   "paper.citation: placeholder pages from '2025;0:1-11' (Epub ahead of print) removed -> 'Br J Sports Med. 2025.'",
   "sports: Soccer appears in only one study -> replaced with American Football, Ice Hockey and Other Sport (Australian football, cricket, baseball) alongside Rugby; populations: added Collegiate (NCAA Division 1 studies)",
   "paper.findings/limitations: added inter-rater reliability results, mechanism findings and Premier League funding and employment",
   "paper.rtp/athleteDev: reframed from clearance to identification and removal ('Relevant to concussion identification ... not return-to-play progression')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The study was funded by the Premier League and three authors were Premier League employees at the time; the conclusions read as cautious but a reviewer may want to note the funding when presenting it to staff.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat headgear as an established concussion prevention measure for female athletes, when the only protective estimate is very low certainty, combines different headgear types, and comes from adolescent lacrosse and soccer.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Shill IJ, Shepherd HA, Eliason PH, Kolstad AT, Heyward O, Martens G, et al.   "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2025-109915",
  "abstract": "Systematic review with meta-analyses and GRADE of 108 studies on prevention strategies (67) and modifiable risk factors (41) for sport-related concussion and head impact events in female, woman and girl athletes.   "tldr": "Evidence for concussion prevention strategies and risk factors specific to female, woman and girl athletes is thin. The only protective signal is very low certainty support for headgear in adolescent lacrosse and soccer, while eyewear and artificial turf showed no concussion effect.",
  "methods": "PRISMA systematic review with meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD42023485808) searching eight databases (Medline, CINAHL, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, EMBASE, ERIC, CENTRAL and CDSR) from 2001 to October and November 2023. Br J Sports Med 2023;57:749-61' as reference 13, the earlier aggregate-data review in which only 3% of studies were female focused. A correction notice says the title was amended after Online First.",

 }

 "sourceFile": "Acute-chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports - a multilevel meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis' matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896651 is printed in the header and citation box.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and three-level multilevel meta-analysis of observational studies in competitive team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, and elevated acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) showed a small-to-moderate association with injury (Hedges g 0.35, 95% CI 0.16-0.54; I2 = 95.8%), stronger for contact and non-contact injuries and near null for time-loss injuries.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Heterogeneity was very high (I2 = 95.8%), several moderator analyses rested on few studies, and ACWR calculation methods, time windows, load metrics, injury definitions and pre-injury exclusion windows varied. The evidence is observational with possible reverse causation, so it shows association only and cannot establish causation or prediction.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled g of 0.35 as a 35% increase in injury risk, which the authors explicitly reject, and treat ACWR as a stand-alone injury predictor or threshold, which they also reject.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2026,
  "citation": "Ding L, Weldon A, Xu J, Malone S, Sampaio J, Zhang Z, et al. Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2026;14:1896651.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896651",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the association between acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in team-sport athletes. Of 41 eligible studies, 16 (797 athletes) were pooled, showing a small-to-moderate association with injury (g = 0.35) and very high heterogeneity.",
  "tldr": "In team-sport athletes, a high acute:chronic workload ratio was associated with somewhat higher injury risk, most clearly for contact and non-contact injuries. The authors conclude it is a contextual monitoring flag within a multi-marker load-management approach, not a stand-alone predictor or threshold.",
  "methods": "PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to 28 October 2024, with supplementary Google Scholar, ResearchGate and reference-list searches; English only. Cohort studies (prospective or retrospective), trials and other longitudinal studies of competitive team-sport athletes reporting ACWR and injury were eligible; effect sizes were converted to Hedges g and pooled with a three-level random-effects model, with moderator analyses, Newcastle-Ottawa quality ratings and Egger and trim-and-fill tests. {
 "id": "Q16",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.3390/nu17213475 is printed in the citation box and page footer.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and fixed-effects meta-analysis of 13 placebo-controlled studies (6 male-only, 6 female-only, 1 mixed; samples of 10 to 52) on acute caffeine and repeated sprint ability (RSA) peak power output, with running sprint times converted to power by formula. Caffeine increased peak power versus placebo (WMD 5.28, 95% CI 2.49-8.07; I2 = 7%), with a significant effect at 6 mg/kg or more (WMD 6.67, 95% CI 3.32-10.02) but not at lower doses (WMD 2.16, 95% CI -2.87 to 7.19).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Small crossover samples, a fixed-effects model, and running sprint times converted to peak power make the pooled values hard to interpret in real units. No formal tests of subgroup differences are reported for dose, modality or sex, and adverse effects were not analyzed.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the pooled benefit as applying to any dose and any sprint test, when the lower-dose estimate crosses zero, the paper contradicts itself on whether cycling or running showed the larger effect, and match performance was not tested.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Wang Y, Su W, Zhang S, Zhao L, Lv Y, Gu B, et al. Effects of Acute Caffeine Ingestion on Repeated Sprint Ability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nutrients. 2025;17:3475.",
  "doi": "10.3390/nu17213475",
  "abstract": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies on acute caffeine and repeated sprint ability. Caffeine improved peak power output compared with placebo, with a significant effect at doses of 6 mg/kg or more but not at lower doses, and significant effects within both male and female subgroups.",
  "tldr": "Caffeine taken about 60 minutes before testing improved repeated sprint peak power, and the benefit was significant at 6 mg/kg or more but not at 3 to 5 mg/kg. The studies used lab sprint tests with small samples, so match-play effects and side effects were not assessed.",
  "methods": "PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251150247) of PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane Library, Web of Science and Scopus from inception to 6 September 2025, including acute caffeine versus placebo studies with peak power output as the primary outcome. Fastest running sprint times were converted to peak power with a formula, data were pooled as weighted mean differences with fixed-effects models, and subgroups by dose, modality and sex were examined; risk of bias used the Cochrane tool and PEDro, and certainty used GRADE.",
  "findings": "Caffeine increased RSA peak power output versus placebo (WMD 5.28, 95% CI 2.49-8.07; p = 0.0002; I2 = 7%). Doses of 6 mg/kg or more gave a significant effect (WMD 6.67, 95% CI 3.32-10.02) and lower doses did not (WMD 2.16, 95% CI -2.87 to 7.19, p = 0.40). Effects were significant within cycling (WMD 8.77) and running (WMD 4.56) protocols and within males (WMD 13.11) and females (WMD 4.03), and the authors rated overall certainty as high.",
  "limitations": "Only powder and capsule caffeine were included and not analyzed separately, and training status and habitual caffeine intake were not controlled. The abstract says cycling showed the larger effect (8.77 vs 4.56) while the results and discussion say running did, and no between-subgroup tests are reported for modality or sex, so the 'no significant sex difference' statement is the authors' assertion. The funnel plot showed substantial asymmetry, and adverse effects (higher at 9 mg/kg in one study) were not analyzed.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors recommend 6 mg/kg taken 60 minutes before exercise as an evidence-based strategy for repeated sprint peak power; 9 mg/kg did not add benefit in comparison studies and was linked to more side effects. Lower doses (3 to 5 mg/kg) did not show a significant pooled benefit, though individual studies varied, possibly with habitual caffeine use.",
  "athleteDev": "Sports nutrition staff can consider about 6 mg/kg caffeine 60 minutes before repeated sprint work, with attention to individual tolerance and side effects that this review did not assess. The outcome is lab RSA peak power, so transfer to match running still needs checking.",
  "rtp": "Not designed for return to sport: included studies tested healthy participants, including some adolescent samples, on RSA performance, so the review cannot inform caffeine use during rehabilitation or after injury."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.limitations: said caffeine was given in several forms including mouth rinse and drinks -> only powder and capsule forms were included ('the present analysis included only powder and capsule forms without distinguishing their effects separately')",
   "evidenceSummary/findings: 'cycling protocols outperformed running' and 'higher doses outperformed lower doses' implied tested comparisons -> reported as within-subgroup effects; noted the abstract vs results contradiction ('with running-based RSA exhibiting a more pronounced effect') and absent subgroup-difference tests",
   "paper.methods: added fixed-effects pooling ('Data were pooled using fixed-effects models'), formula conversion of running sprint times to power, search date 6 September 2025, Cochrane, PEDro and GRADE",
   "paper.practicalImplications/athleteDev: '6 mg/kg or more' -> 6 mg/kg, the authors' stated dose ('acute caffeine ingestion at 6 mg/kg BW, administered 60 min pre-exercise'); added 9 mg/kg side-effect note and that adverse effects were not analyzed",
   "paper.rtp: 'healthy adults' -> healthy participants including adolescent samples (mean ages 16.7, 16.9 and 18.3 years in three female studies)",
   "paper.tldr: removed 'no significant sex difference' as a finding, since no between-sex test is reported"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The authors rate certainty as high despite small samples, substantial funnel plot asymmetry and an internal contradiction on modality; a reviewer may wish to temper that rating. The WMD units are not stated and include formula-converted running data.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}
